sections.title: How does the Mega Millions payout calculator work?
sections.html:
The Mega Millions payout calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports annual growth rate in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the payout frequency, the annuity payout option and the type of annuity); then you give the dates it asks for; then you type in the annuity rate, the lump sum payout percentage, the inflation rate and the annuity payout.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• How much did you win?: a plain number with no unit attached.
  • Annuity rate: a measured quantity, entered by default in percent. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • What is your filing status?: pick the option that matches your case — 4 options, such as single, married filing jointly and married filing separately. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Where do you live?: pick the option that matches your case — 51 options, such as alabama, alaska and arizona. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Lump sum payout percentage: a measured quantity, entered by default in percent. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • Payout frequency: pick the option that matches your case — 6 options, such as yearly, semi-annually and quarterly. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Inflation rate: a measured quantity, entered by default in percent. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • Set term by: pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as length and dates. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Final payout on: a calendar date. Use the picker; the answer is recalculated the moment the date changes, and the count is done date-to-date rather than by subtracting timestamps.
  • Annuity payout option: pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as fixed payment annuity and fixed length annuity. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Annuity payout: a measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.
  • Final balance: a measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.
  • Length of annuity: a measured quantity, entered by default in years. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • Show me: pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as monthly schedule and yearly schedule. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Display: pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as chart of balances, table of payment schedule and show all. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Type of annuity: pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as ordinary annuity and annuity due. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Compounding method: pick the option that matches your case — 7 options, such as yearly, semi-annually and quarterly. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Periodic growth rate: a measured quantity, entered by default in percent. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.

9 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Mega Millions payout calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Annual growth rate=(periodic growth rate + 1 ^ payout frequency) − 1
Starting from=rounded down, (final payout on...)
Gross cash=(lump sum payout percentage × how much did you win?)
Tax fed cash 24=((6 ÷ 25) × (lump sum payout percentage × how much did you win?))
Net cash 24=((lump sum payout percentage × how much did you win?) − ((6 ÷ 25) × (lump sum payout percentage × how much did you win?)))
Tax fed cash ph=(((lump sum payout percentage × how much did you win?), var stat) − ((6 ÷ 25) × (lump sum payout percentage × how much did you win?)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Annuity rate: %, opening in percent
  • Lump sum payout percentage: %, opening in percent
  • Inflation rate: %, opening in percent
  • Annuity payout: Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Final balance: Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Annual growth rate: %, opening in percent
  • Length of annuity: Time, opening in years
  • Periodic growth rate: %, opening in percent

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Mega Millions payout calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the annuity rate, the lump sum payout percentage and the inflation rate — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Dates are compared date to date in your own time zone, so a daylight-saving change will not shift the count by a day.

faq.q: What does the Mega Millions payout calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns annual growth rate, derived from the annuity rate, the lump sum payout percentage and the inflation rate. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Mega Millions payout calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the annuity rate, the lump sum payout percentage and the inflation rate, which is 18 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter annuity rate in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Annuity rate opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (9 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Mega Millions payout calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
